h1: The 8 Best Monitors Under $100 for Home Offices, Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: 8 monitors under $100 compared on panel type, size, refresh rate, ports and eye-care features for home offices.
summary: The Philips 241V8LB is the best monitor under $100 for most desks, with a sharp 23.8 inch VA panel and 100Hz. The Lenovo L22-4e is the best IPS option, the MSI MP225 has the smoothest 120Hz motion, and the Sceptre Prime 24 inch has the most inputs.
intro: Screen size is the first thing shoppers check, and under $100 it is the thing most likely to disappoint. A 27 inch monitor at 1080p stretches the same pixels across a larger surface, so text looks softer than it does on a 24 inch. We ranked these eight monitors by panel type, resolution, size and inputs together, not by inches alone.

We reviewed eight monitors from their listings, all in the $50 to $100 band, so every one sits near the upper half of this budget. Where a listing omits the panel type or resolution, we say so. Refresh and response figures are manufacturer claims.

products.name: Philips 241V8LB 24 Inch FHD 100Hz VA Monitor
products.verdict: A 23.8 inch Full HD VA panel with 100Hz, flicker-free backlighting and a paper-like reading mode.
products.description:
The Philips 241V8LB is a 23.8 inch 1920 by 1080 monitor with a VA panel, a 100Hz refresh rate, 178 degree viewing angles and a three-side near-borderless frame. It adds EasyRead mode for long documents, flicker-free backlighting and VESA mounting. At about 21.3 inches wide, it suits most desks.

It ranks first because it combines the contrast of a VA panel with a sensible size and resolution. At 23.8 inches, 1080p keeps text sharp, which is not true of the 27 inch models below. Against the Lenovo it gives deeper blacks, while the Lenovo gives better viewing angles and a published sRGB number.

Buy it for an office desk, general browsing and streaming. Its price band is $50 to $100, so it can reach the top of the budget. The caveat is that VA panels smear dark motion more than IPS, and there is no stated color gamut.
products.idealFor: Office users who want a clean, sharp everyday display.
products.skipIf: You need accurate color for photo work.

products.name: Lenovo L22-4e 21.5 Inch FHD IPS 100Hz Monitor
products.verdict: A 21.5 inch IPS panel with 99% sRGB, 100Hz and a tilt stand.
products.description:
The L22-4e is a 21.5 inch Full HD IPS display with 100Hz, a 4ms response in extreme mode, 99% sRGB and a 1300:1 contrast ratio. It has a three-sided borderless design, 178 degree viewing angles, a tilt-only stand and VESA mounting.

It ranks second because IPS gives truer color from side angles and the 99% sRGB claim is verifiable, which Philips does not offer. The 1300:1 contrast is a step behind VA panels such as the MSI, and the stand only tilts, so you may want an arm. It beats the MSI for color work.

Buy it if you do light photo edits or share the screen with colleagues. It falls in the $50 to $100 price band. The caveat is the smaller 21.5 inch size and the lack of height adjustment.
products.idealFor: Light creative users who want verified color and wide angles.
products.skipIf: You want a large 27 inch screen.

products.name: MSI PRO MP225 E12VL 22 Inch FHD 120Hz VA Monitor
products.verdict: A 120Hz VA monitor with 4000:1 contrast and TUV flicker-free certification.
products.description:
MSI's MP225 E12VL is a 21.45 inch Full HD VA monitor with 120Hz, Adaptive-Sync, a 4000:1 contrast ratio, TUV Rheinland flicker-free and low blue light certification, an Eye-Q Check tool and VESA 100 by 100 mounting. It has an HDMI input and an accessory slot.

It sits third because the 120Hz panel is the smoothest in this guide, but it is small at 21.45 inches and the listing names only an HDMI port. The 4000:1 contrast is the best claim here and gives it deep blacks. It beats the Sceptre 100Hz models on motion, and the TUV certification is a third-party mark, which most rivals lack.

Buy it if you game casually or want a smoother cursor. Its price band is $50 to $100.
products.idealFor: Casual gamers and anyone who values smooth scrolling.

products.name: Sceptre Prime 24 Inch 100Hz Gaming Monitor, DisplayPort, HDMI x2
products.verdict: A 24 inch 1080p 100Hz monitor with DisplayPort, two HDMI and 100% sRGB.
products.description:
Sceptre's 24 inch Prime has 1920 by 1080 resolution, a 100Hz refresh rate, 1ms blur reduction, 100% sRGB, FreeSync, DisplayPort and two HDMI 2.0 ports, built-in speakers and a VESA wall mount pattern. It adds Blue Light Shift and FPS and RTS game presets.

It ranks fourth because of its inputs: DisplayPort plus two HDMI beats the VGA-equipped siblings. The built-in speakers are an add-on, not a strength, and the panel type is not stated on this listing, which weakens the case next to Philips and Lenovo. It beats its 24 inch FreeSync sibling by adding the 100% sRGB claim.

Buy it if you connect a console and a PC at once. It sits in the $50 to $100 price band. The caveat is that speakers at this price are thin, so plan on headphones.
products.idealFor: Anyone connecting a PC and a console to one screen.
products.skipIf: You want a stated IPS or VA panel.

products.name: Sceptre Prime 27 Inch 100Hz Gaming Monitor, DisplayPort, 100% sRGB
products.verdict: A large 27 inch 100Hz screen with DisplayPort and two HDMI, at the same price tier.
products.description:
Sceptre's 27 inch Prime has a 100Hz refresh rate with 1ms response, 100% sRGB, FreeSync, DisplayPort and two HDMI ports, built-in speakers, Blue Light Shift, game presets and a VESA mount. At about 24 inches wide it is a big panel.

It ranks fifth because the listing does not spell out the resolution, so check it before buying: on a 27 inch screen, lower resolutions look soft for text. It offers the most screen area here for the money, and the inputs match the 24 inch DisplayPort model. It beats the VGA 27 inch on connections.

Buy it for a big, immersive desk display for video and games. Its price band is $50 to $100.
cons: Text may look soft at this size
products.idealFor: People who want the biggest screen for the budget.
products.skipIf: You do a lot of text work on a 1080p panel.

products.name: Sceptre 24 Inch 100Hz Gaming Monitor, FreeSync, 2x HDMI, DisplayPort
products.verdict: A 24 inch 100Hz FreeSync monitor with 1ms blur reduction and built-in speakers.
products.description:
This Sceptre 24 inch has a 100Hz refresh rate, 1ms blur reduction, FreeSync, two HDMI ports, one DisplayPort, Blue Light Shift, an edgeless design and built-in speakers.

It lands sixth because it overlaps with the Prime 24 inch and does not list a sRGB figure. The listing gives fewer panel details than Philips or Lenovo.

Buy it if it is the cheapest of the Sceptre 24 inch options when you shop. Its price band is $50 to $100.
products.idealFor: Shoppers comparing Sceptre prices who want a 24 inch.

products.name: Sceptre Prime 24 Inch 100Hz Monitor, 100% sRGB, 2x HDMI, VGA
products.verdict: A 24 inch monitor that adds a VGA port for older computers.
products.description:
This Sceptre 24 inch Prime has 100% sRGB, two HDMI ports and a VGA port, built-in speakers, Blue Light Shift and FPS and RTS presets. The 100Hz refresh rate is listed.

It ranks seventh because there is no DisplayPort and the VGA port limits the picture quality of anything plugged into it. Its value is for people with an older PC or projector that still needs VGA.

Buy it for legacy hardware. Its price band is $50 to $100.
products.idealFor: Offices with older computers or projectors.

products.name: Sceptre Prime 27 Inch 100Hz Monitor, 2x HDMI, VGA, 99% sRGB
products.verdict: A 27 inch 100Hz screen with 99% sRGB, edgeless styling and VESA mounting.
products.description:
This Sceptre 27 inch lists 100Hz, 1ms blur reduction, 99% sRGB, two HDMI ports and a VGA port, built-in speakers, edgeless design and VESA wall mounting.

It comes last because it has no DisplayPort and no stated resolution, and it duplicates the 27 inch DisplayPort model with fewer inputs. It is for buyers who want a large screen and have no need for DisplayPort.

Buy it if the larger panel is the priority. Its price band is $50 to $100.
products.idealFor: Buyers who want a big screen over a fast port.

methodology.title: Panel type
methodology.description: We compared IPS and VA panels, and noted where the listing does not state the type.

methodology.title: Resolution and size
methodology.description: Screen size was set against resolution, since 1080p on 27 inches is softer than on 24 inches.

methodology.title: Refresh and response
methodology.description: 100Hz and 120Hz claims, blur reduction and adaptive sync support were weighed.

methodology.title: Inputs and ergonomics
methodology.description: DisplayPort, HDMI and VGA ports were counted, along with stand adjustment and VESA support.

methodology.title: Value under $100
methodology.description: Every monitor sits in the $50 to $100 band, so the top end of the budget applies to all of them.

whatMatters.detail: IPS panels hold color and brightness from the side, and VA panels offer deeper blacks with a narrower sweet spot. TN is cheapest and weakest. A listing that names IPS or VA gives you confidence, and one that does not is hiding a likely compromise.

Text sharpness depends on pixels per inch. A 1080p panel looks crisp at 22 to 24 inches and softens at 27. If the listing leaves out resolution on a 27 inch screen, check before buying, and prefer 24 inches for text-heavy work.

60Hz is standard, while 100 to 120Hz makes scrolling and mouse movement look smoother. It matters more than most people expect, even for office work. Make sure your cable and port can carry it, since HDMI 1.4 may not.
HDMI covers most uses, DisplayPort is better for high refresh on a PC, and VGA is analog and softer. Count the ports against what you connect, such as a laptop, console and streaming box.
Budget monitors often come with tilt-only stands. A VESA 75 or 100 pattern lets you add an arm for height and swivel. If you sit for hours, plan for an arm or a stack of books.

faq.q: Will these work with my laptop?
faq.a: Any laptop with an HDMI port can drive the 100Hz models, though HDMI version limits refresh. DisplayPort or USB-C needs a cable or adapter.

faq.q: What is the most common mistake?
faq.a: Buying a 27 inch 1080p screen for text work. The pixels look larger and softer, so choose 24 inches or a higher resolution.

faq.q: Is the Philips worth it over the Lenovo?
faq.a: If you prefer contrast and size, yes. If you want IPS angles and a stated 99% sRGB, the Lenovo is the better fit.
Use a good HDMI or DisplayPort cable, then open the display settings on your computer and choose the highest refresh rate.

faq.q: How do I clean the screen?
faq.a: Turn it off and use a dry microfiber cloth. For marks, use a cloth dampened with water, never spray the panel.

faq.q: Can I mount these on an arm?
faq.a: Most list VESA 75 or 100 mounting. Check the pattern and weight against the arm you plan to use.

finalTake: The Philips 241V8LB is the best monitor under $100 for general use because it gives a sharp 1080p picture at a sensible size. Choose the Lenovo if you want IPS color, the MSI for 120Hz motion, and the Sceptre Prime 24 inch if you need DisplayPort and two HDMI. Check resolution before buying any 27 inch screen.
